retrieved.title: proof-theory-development

Although Gödel’s incompleteness theorems demonstrated that full consistency proofs were unattainable within finitary systems, Gentzen achieved significant success by using transfinite induction and sequent calculus to prove the consistency of Peano arithmetic. This development shifted the field toward analyzing proof structures via ordinal analysis and expanded its applications into computer science.

This foundational project relied on Basic Law V, which was subsequently invalidated by Russell's Paradox, exposing a fatal contradiction in his system. Despite this failure, his work established rigorous logical structures for language and mathematics that remain central to modern philosophy.

He treated existence as a second-level concept, interpreting existential claims as assertions about concepts rather than objects falling under them. Additionally, Frege addressed puzzles regarding cognitive significance in identity statements and propositional attitudes.

This theoretical framework was further refined through contributions from Skolem, Herbrand, and Péter, ultimately establishing the robust class of effectively computable functions. These developments laid the groundwork for the modern field of recursion theory initiated by Kleene.

retrieved.title: recursive-functions
retrieved.snippet: The passages argue that recursive function theory and computability theory are foundational to mathematical logic, establishing that effectively computable functions coincide with general recursive functions as posited by Church's Thesis. This theoretical framework supports rigorous proofs regarding the Entscheidungsproblem and enables the classification of functions based on their absolute and relative computability properties. Key developments include the distinction between primitive and partial recursive functions, the Normal Form Theorem, and the study of non-computable total functions.

retrieved.title: recursive-functions

It then extends this framework to partial recursive functions by introducing unbounded minimization, distinguishing total recursive functions from general partial ones. Finally, it connects these computational classes to logical definability, characterizing computable and computably enumerable relations through Delta-0-1 and Sigma-0-1 formulas respectively.

retrieved.title: recursive-functions

retrieved.title: recursive-functions

This framework is supported by demonstrating how basic functions, such as addition and primality testing, can be constructed using initial functions and closure properties like composition and recursion. These developments establish the class of effectively computable functions and connect them to broader concepts in computability theory, including Gödel's incompleteness results and Kleene’s T-predicate.

retrieved.title: computability
retrieved.snippet: Primitive recursive functions are defined as the smallest class closed under composition and primitive recursion, encompassing basic arithmetic operations but excluding all computable functions. To capture the full scope of computability, Gödel extended this framework by adding the unbounded minimization operator to form the set of general Recursive functions. This extension allows for the computation of total functions that cannot be derived through primitive recursion alone.

retrieved.snippet: illumination  Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 CE) was influential in pushing the separate-and-divine reading of De anima III.5, and Islamic philosophers (most notably Ibn Sīnā [980–1037] and Ibn Rushd [c.1126–c.1198]) would later follow suit. Themistius (4th century CE), in contrast, championed the part-of-soul reading, and Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) would second this interpretation. retrieved.snippet: tibbon  6. Averroes and ‘Abd Allah, “Three Treatises on Conjunction”  The translation of three short treatises on conjunction with the active intellect by Averroes and Averroes’ son ‘Abd Allah was also a pioneering project. They were the first works of Averroes rendered into Hebrew, before any of the commentaries on Aristotle. Ibn Tibbon translated them and attached them to his commentary on Ecclesiastes. He did this, he maintained, because Averroes and Solomon were aiming to do precisely the same thing: to defend the doctrine of conjunction against skeptics who denied that it was possible.

retrieved.snippet: philip-chancellor  Philip the Chancellor was an influential figure in a number of different circles in the first half of the thirteenth century. He enjoyed a long though rather turbulent ecclesiastical career and was famous for his sermons and his lyric poetry, the latter of which has received attention by a number of musicologists in recent years (see Dronke 1987, Payne 1991, Traill 2003). retrieved.title: ibn-rushd
retrieved.snippet: ibn-rushd  The Andalusian philosopher, physician and judge Ibn Rushd (1126–1198) is one of the great figures of philosophy within the Muslim contexts, and a foundational source for post-classical European thought.

retrieved.title: ibn-rushd
retrieved.snippet: ibn-rushd  The hallmarks of Ibn Rushd’s work are his convictions that philosophy is capable of demonstrative certainty in many domains, that it is Aristotle who should be our preeminent guide in philosophy, and that philosophy should play a central role within religious inquiry, rather than being an alternative to religion. But part of what gives his ideas their enduring interest is the subtle way in which he promotes other methods of reasoning and persuasion in contexts where the rigors of Aristotelian demonstration are not a practical option. retrieved.title: ibn-rushd
retrieved.snippet: ibn-rushd  Abū al-Walīd Muḥammad ibn Ahmad Ibn Rushd was born in Cordova in 1126. He belonged to an influential Andalusian family, famous for its judicial power and for its scholarship in the religious sciences. His father was a prominent judge, but the most important figure in the family was his grandfather, who also bears his name, Ibn Rushd, and so the philosopher is called “the grandson” (al-ḥafīd) to distinguish him from his grandfather (al-jadd). The latter was both a well-known judge and a famed jurist, being the author of many books in jurisprudence following the Mālikī school.

retrieved.title: ibn-rushd-natural
retrieved.snippet: ibn-rushd-natural  Philosophy has been divided into theoretical and practical since the time of Aristotle’s distinction of the sciences, and within theoretical philosophy, the enquire on nature was of major import in Ancient and Medieval times. Most of its contents later developed into modern natural science as the seeds of physics or chemistry, but its founding concepts are still worth reflecting upon. Concepts such as those of body and extension, motion and change, time and place, finiteness and infiniteness, and of nature itself have kept their philosophical gist.

retrieved.snippet: ibn-arabi  Ibn ‘Arabî (1165–1240) can be considered the greatest of all Muslim philosophers, provided we understand philosophy in the broad, modern sense and not simply as the discipline of falsafa, whose outstanding representatives are Avicenna and, many would say, Mullâ Sadrâ. retrieved.title: ibn-arabi
retrieved.snippet: ibn-arabi  Ibn ‘Arabî’s writings remained unknown in the West until modern times, but they spread throughout the Islamic world within a century of his death. The early Orientalists, with one or two exceptions, paid little attention to him because he had no discernable influence in Europe. His works, moreover, are notoriously difficult, making it easy to dismiss him as a “mystic” or a “pantheist” without trying to read him. retrieved.title: medieval-philosophy
retrieved.snippet: medieval-philosophy  “Medieval philosophy” has changed its meaning among specialists over the last twenty years. The change is not in chronology, where views remain divided (see  §5):  most agree that the period stretches at least from 500–1500, but some push the starting point back and/or the end point forward.
